title: Confidence
full_review:
After inadvertently ripping off a crime boss, a tight-knit group of con men is forced to pull off a more complicated scam in the slick but shallow caper, "Confidence" (Lions Gate).

Jake Vig (Ed Burns) heads the team of crooks, who in collaboration with two dirty cops (Donal Logue and Luis Guzman) stage a fake homicide and end up with a case of cash when their terrified mark races off during the shootout.

The next day, however, when both the mark and one of the con men turn up dead, Jake discovers they have stolen from crime lord King (Dustin Hoffman), so goes to make amends. Jake is ordered to execute a much more elaborate sting as repayment, the target being King's hated, money-launderer nemesis (Robert Forster).

Cocky Jake decides to go for an even bigger take than the amount owed King, and enlists a comely pickpocket (Rachel Weisz) to mesmerize and manipulate males where needed. However, a federal agent (Andy Garcia) long on Jake's trail surfaces and begins closing in on the gang just as the sting is getting under way.

As directed by James Foley, the caper involves a complicated series of offshore wire transfers and corporate loans that, as the genre demands, call for further twists and double-crosses. The narrative is intriguingly structured in Doug Jung's screenplay but its self-satisfied tone and smug admiration for its brutal, criminal characters should not endear it to viewers. Not only are the crooks extremely greedy, but show no hesitation to kill to get the big bucks.

When such films are presented as simply a comic fantasy, a crime-does-pay conclusion can be taken with a grain of salt, but "Confidence" comes across as grounded in reality and the film seems most impressed with its own vicious cleverness and cynical worldview.

Burns is a cool customer as the lead thief and Hoffman is amusingly outrageous as the unconventional crime kingpin, but in delivering such a shallow, heartless work, the filmmakers were perhaps overconfident.

Due to some violence, brief nudity, seamy sexual situations, recurring profanities and constant rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
